articles.title: iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8: Is $2,000 worth it?
articles.summary: Apple's iPhone Duo reportedly outlasted the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 by over three hours in battery tests, but its weight and repair costs raise concerns.
articles.body: How much would you pay for a phone that turns into a small tablet? Apple is betting the answer is nearly $2,000. After seven years of watching Samsung build folding phones, Apple has finally entered the race with its first-ever foldable iPhone. The new iPhone Duo, which went on sale Oct. 23, opens like a book to reveal a 7.6-inch screen. Its biggest competitor, Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, offers the same screen size and a remarkably similar design. However, Samsung's phone is lighter and costs about $100 less. Apple has some interesting advantages of its own, including impressive battery performance and a clever screen designed to reduce glare. But there are compromises on both sides, including a repair bill that might make you think twice about carrying either phone without protection. So, has Apple finally cracked the folding phone formula, or does Samsung still have the better idea? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. 8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT Apple enters the foldable phone race seven years late Samsung introduced the original Galaxy Fold in 2019. Those early devices came with plenty of growing pains, including concerns about screen durability. Since then, Samsung has steadily improved its folding technology. Apple took its time. In fact, we covered one of the company's early ideas in our article about Apple's foldable iPhone patent in 2023. Now the iPhone Duo is finally here, and Apple has made some interesting design decisions. The phone features a polished titanium frame, Apple's A20 Pro processor and a large inner OLED display. It also introduces a redesigned version of iOS built around the folding experience. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 takes a different approach. It uses Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip and Samsung's One UI 9 software, which has evolved through several generations of folding phones. That experience gives Samsung an advantage in some areas. However, Apple has already managed to outperform its rival in early battery testing. iPhone Duo vs Galaxy Z Fold 8 price: Prepare for sticker shock Let's get the painful part out of the way. The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for 256GB of storage. The 512GB model costs $2,199, while the 1TB version jumps to $2,599. If you really want to splurge, Apple's 2TB model costs an eye-watering $3,199. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts at $1,899.99 for 256GB. The 512GB version costs $2,099.99, while the 1TB model reaches $2,499.99. That puts Samsung roughly $100 below Apple at comparable storage levels. Of course, Samsung has another advantage. Its Fold 8 has been on sale since August, so retailers and carriers have had time to introduce promotions. However, I'd look closely at those deals before celebrating the savings. Some carrier offers require a qualifying trade-in or a lengthy commitment to monthly bill credits. There's also a larger question. When you're already spending nearly $2,000, will saving $100 really determine which phone you choose? I suspect the answer comes down to what happens when you actually hold them. Apple's folding iPhone has a weight problem One of the first things you'll notice about these phones is how similar they look. Both fold horizontally like a book, with smaller screens on the outside and expansive displays when opened. But there's a noticeable difference in weight. The iPhone Duo weighs 8.96 ounces, compared with 7.09 ounces for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's almost two ounces heavier for Apple's phone. If you've ever carried a heavy smartphone in your pocket all day, you know how noticeable that can become. The difference could be even more apparent when you're holding the phone open for extended periods. Samsung also wins on thickness. Its Fold 8 measures about 0.38 inches thick when closed, while the Duo measures 0.44 inches. Apple counters with a rounded titanium design that may feel more comfortable in your hand. Samsung uses sharper edges and a flatter appearance. There's also something worth thinking about. Both phones have relatively small outer screens. Apple's measures 5.4 inches, while Samsung's comes in at 5.5 inches. Those screens are perfectly usable for everyday tasks. However, they're considerably smaller than the displays on many conventional flagship phones. You could end up spending $2,000 on a device that requires an extra step whenever you want a bigger screen. That's why I'd recommend trying both in person before buying. The phone that feels exciting for five minutes in a store needs to feel comfortable after five hours in your hand. The iPhone Duo display has a clever trick Both folding phones open to reveal 7.6-inch OLED screens with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. Each also offers peak outdoor brightness of 3,000 nits. The real difference comes down to how those displays handle reflections. Apple developed a nano-texture finish for the Duo's inner screen. It creates a matte appearance that helps reduce glare and makes the fold crease harder to see. Anyone who has struggled to read a glossy screen near a sunny window might appreciate this approach. Samsung's screen has a more traditional glossy finish, which can make colors appear richer. Some early iPhone Duo reviews suggest Apple's matte display sacrifices a little contrast and vibrancy to achieve its reduced reflections. Neither approach will appeal to everyone. However, Apple has another interesting feature coming. Apple Pencil support could give the Duo an edge The iPhone Duo now supports the Apple Pencil (USB-C) through iOS 27.2, which Apple released on Oct. 26. That means you can sketch or annotate documents directly on the folding screen. The feature already works in the software's release candidate. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 does not support the S Pen. Samsung removed the feature as it pursued thinner folding designs. There is one catch with Apple's approach. The Duo works only with the USB-C Apple Pencil. Even if you already own an Apple Pencil Pro, you won't be able to use it with this phone. The USB-C version also lacks the pressure sensitivity available on more advanced Apple Pencil models. Still, this could be useful for someone who regularly signs documents or prefers handwritten notes. Samsung still understands multitasking better Here's where those seven years of Samsung experience become apparent. Let's say you're on a video call and someone sends you an important document. You want to review it without interrupting the conversation. Then you need to check your calendar. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 can handle several apps on its larger screen. You can run three apps in split-screen mode, and Samsung also offers pop-up windows for additional flexibility. The Fold 8 supports Samsung DeX, too, giving you a desktop-style experience when connected to compatible external displays. Apple has introduced Split View on the Duo, allowing two apps to run side by side. That's a first for the iPhone, and it should make the larger screen far more useful. However, Apple's approach remains more restrictive than Samsung's. Split View uses a fixed arrangement, and you don't get the same floating-window flexibility. There's another issue that early iPhone Duo owners are discovering. Some iPhone apps aren't ready for the bigger screen Apple redesigned iOS 27 for the Duo, which ships with iOS 27.1. Its own apps have been adapted to use the folding display. However, some third-party apps haven't caught up. Early reviewers found that certain apps display large black bars or awkward layouts when opened on the bigger screen. That could be frustrating when you've paid so much for additional screen space. Fortunately, developers can update their apps to support the Duo's design. Some popular apps have already received updates, and more are expected. For now, though, Samsung has a more established folding software experience. I would also pay attention to which apps you use most. A larger screen loses some of its appeal when your favorite apps still behave as though they're running on a much smaller phone. Apple's battery life delivers a welcome surprise Folding phones have a difficult job. They need enough battery power to run a large display without becoming too bulky. Apple's iPhone Duo uses two internal batteries and an A20 Pro processor designed for efficient performance. Samsung equips its Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a 4,800mAh battery and Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip. Both processors offer plenty of power for demanding apps. However, early independent testing suggests Apple has a surprising advantage when it comes to battery life. In one battery test involving continuous web browsing over 5G, the iPhone Duo reportedly lasted 13 hours and 20 minutes, compared with 10 hours and 6 minutes for Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8. That's more than three additional hours for Apple. Another independent test produced encouraging results for the Duo. While streaming video over Wi-Fi with the larger screens at maximum brightness, Apple's foldable reportedly lasted 18 hours and 15 minutes, compared with 16 hours and 30 minutes for Samsung. Although the tests used different methods, both suggest Apple has managed to squeeze impressive battery life out of its first folding phone. Apple officially claims up to 31 hours of video playback using the inner display. However, that figure comes from controlled laboratory testing, so everyday results will vary depending on how you use the phone. Charging is another consideration. Apple says the Duo can reach 50% in about 20 minutes with a compatible wired charger. Samsung supports 45W wired charging and fast wireless charging. For anyone who spends long days traveling or regularly finds their battery running low before dinner, Apple's early results are encouraging. THE IPHONE DUO IS OFFICIALLY HERE — GET IT FOR NO MONEY DOWN AT T-MOBILE A $2,000 folding phone still comes with camera compromises For nearly $2,000, you'd expect a phone with an incredible camera. And while both of these foldables take excellent photos, there's a catch. Apple's iPhone Duo has two 48MP rear cameras, while Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 has two 50MP cameras. Neither has a dedicated telephoto lens, which means you're giving up some of the zoom capabilities found on other premium phones. Think about trying to get a close-up shot of your child playing soccer or capturing something interesting in the distance while on vacation. Apple's Duo offers 2x optical-quality zoom by cropping into its main sensor. Samsung uses a similar approach, with digital zoom for subjects farther away. Both can handle everyday photos, but if you love getting those close-up shots, an iPhone 18 Pro Max or Galaxy S26 Ultra may be a better choice. Here's where Samsung throws another option into the mix. Its Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra starts at $2,099.99, just $100 more than Apple's Duo at their regular starting prices. For that extra money, you get a 200MP main camera and a dedicated telephoto lens with 3x optical zoom. That's worth considering if you want a folding phone but aren't willing to give up a more versatile camera. And with Samsung already offering discounts on some models, you may not even have to spend more. Apple has some fun camera features Samsung can't match exactly Ever try taking a group photo and realize you're the one missing from it? Apple's Smart Take could help with that. Just prop open the iPhone Duo, get into the picture and let its AI recognize when everyone is posing. The phone automatically snaps the photo, so there's no racing against a timer or asking someone else to take the shot. Then there's Duo Preview, which lets the person you're photographing see themselves on the outside screen. That could save you from hearing, "Wait, let me see that one," after every picture. Apple also came up with Kid Cue, which plays Peanuts animations on the outer display to get children to look toward the camera. If you've ever tried getting a toddler to cooperate for a family photo, you can probably appreciate that one. Samsung has a few tricks of its own. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 can show people a preview on its outer screen, and you can prop it partially open for hands-free photos. That comes in handy when you want to be in the picture instead of always being the one taking it. The most expensive iPhone Duo surprise could come after you buy it Now let's talk about something that deserves far more attention than it usually receives. Repairs. Apple rates the iPhone Duo IP68 for dust and water resistance, while Samsung gives the Galaxy Z Fold 8 an IP48 rating. That gives Apple stronger protection against dust under standardized laboratory testing. However, neither rating guarantees that a folding screen or hinge will survive years of rough treatment. These phones also contain more moving parts than conventional smartphones. And if something goes wrong, the repair costs can be substantial. There's another reason to think carefully about durability. As we reported in our article, Apple confirms iPhone Duo screen problems after launch. Some owners experienced cracks along the inner screen near the hinge within hours or days of purchase, sometimes during initial setup. Apple acknowledged an issue affecting a small number of devices and directed affected customers to contact AppleCare for replacements. The company hasn't identified the cause or disclosed how many phones are affected. An AppleCare+ subscription isn't required to request a replacement for this acknowledged issue. Still, it's something I'd consider before spending nearly $2,000 on a first-generation folding iPhone. According to Apple's published repair estimates, replacing the iPhone Duo's damaged inner display costs $999 without AppleCare+. That's roughly half the cost of the entry-level phone. Apple also lists an estimated $1,499 charge for certain other damage repairs. There is some relief for minor screen damage. Apple's replaceable inner display cover layer costs $49 to replace without AppleCare+, provided the damage is limited to that layer. AppleCare+ can significantly reduce eligible repair charges. For example, an inner display repair is listed at $99 under the coverage, subject to the plan's terms. Of course, the coverage itself adds to the cost of ownership. Samsung's folding phones also have specialized displays and hinges that can be expensive to repair. However, repair pricing varies by model, damage and coverage. This is one area where I'd encourage anyone considering either phone to look beyond the advertised purchase price. After all, a $2,000 phone is expensive enough without worrying about what happens if it slips out of your hand and you're suddenly facing a repair bill approaching $1,000. Another iPhone Duo change could surprise travelers Apple has made the iPhone Duo eSIM-only worldwide. That means you won't find a physical SIM card slot. Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8 supports both eSIM and a physical nano-SIM card, although configurations may vary by market. For most people in the United States, this probably won't be an obstacle. Major carriers support eSIM, and many international providers offer digital plans. However, if you travel frequently and prefer buying physical SIM cards at your destination, Samsung gives you more flexibility. It's worth checking whether your preferred mobile provider supports eSIM before buying the Duo. iPhone Duo or Galaxy Z Fold 8: Which should you buy? If you've been waiting years for a folding iPhone, Apple's Duo is an appealing first attempt. It offers excellent early battery performance, an impressive display and the convenience of staying within Apple's ecosystem. However, I wouldn't overlook Samsung. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is significantly lighter, costs a little less and offers more flexible multitasking. Those advantages could become increasingly important once the excitement of owning a new folding phone wears off. And here's something else to consider. If most of your day involves texting or checking email, you may spend far more time using the smaller outer screen than you expect. The larger display becomes especially useful when you frequently review documents or watch videos while traveling. Before buying either phone, think about how much time you would realistically spend with it unfolded. Also, if you're considering switching between Apple and Samsung, take a look at our guide on how to transfer data to a new iPhone or Android at CyberGuy.com. It can help make the move considerably easier. HERE ARE SOME TIPS ON HOW TO ORGANIZE PHOTOS WITH KEYWORDS ON YOUR PHONE Kurt's key takeaways I have to give Samsung credit. Seven years ago, folding phones seemed like an expensive experiment, and I wasn't convinced they'd ever catch on. But Samsung stuck with the idea, and now Apple has finally joined the party. I like what Apple's done with the iPhone Duo, especially the display and those impressive early battery results. Still, I keep coming back to the price. Nearly $2,000 for a phone that's heavier than Samsung's and doesn't have a dedicated telephoto camera? That's a tough sell. And the possibility of a $999 inner screen repair would certainly make me nervous. I also wouldn't count Samsung out just because Apple has entered the race. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is noticeably lighter, and Samsung has spent years figuring out how to make that larger screen useful. Being able to run more apps at once is a nice advantage, especially if you're someone who likes getting work done on your phone. And let's face it, a lighter phone is something you'll appreciate long after the excitement of showing everyone how it folds has worn off. If I were spending this kind of money, I'd want to see how Apple's first folding iPhone holds up after a few months of everyday use. I'd also want to hold both phones before deciding. But here's what I keep wondering. How often would I really open that larger screen? If I ended up using the smaller outside display most of the day, I'd have a hard time convincing myself that spending $2,000 was worth it. articles.title: Windows 11 is now ‘up to 40 percent faster’ on PCs with 8GB of RAM
articles.summary: A new Windows 11 update is improving memory usage and performance.
articles.body: Microsoft has been doing a lot of work to improve memory usage and increase performance on Windows 11 PCs over the past year. Last month the company revealed Windows 11 is now “more responsive” and runs better on PCs with 8GB of RAM, and now the company is releasing a new update today that includes further memory improvements. “On 8 GB PCs, Windows is now up to 20 percent more responsive, and multitasking is up to 40 percent faster in our lab test,” says Windows chief Pavan Davuluri. One of the key ways Microsoft has achieved better performance on PCs with 8GB of RAM is through compression. [Media: “As a result, Windows can now keep up to 2 GB more of your active data in memory instead of moving it to slower storage, so an app or tab you left open is less likely to reload when you return,” says Davuluri. This compression helps Windows avoid writing data to a virtual memory paging file on a disk, slowing down apps and performance. Microsoft is also making improvements across Windows, Edge, and Microsoft 365 apps that reduce “committed-memory growth by up to 900 MB.” Memory improvements in Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and Outlook alone add up to 360MB of RAM savings. Windows 11 no longer loads widgets on a PC with 8GB of RAM until you open the widgets panel, saving around 200MB of RAM. Inactive tabs in Edge now sleep after 15 minutes, reducing memory consumption further. While Microsoft is shipping an update to Windows 11 with these memory improvements, the company is still working on improving RAM usage in Windows in the coming months. Memory compression will get “smarter and more efficient” over the next few months, and Windows features and apps will share more common parts like widgets and search sharing a single web engine. Microsoft is also working with PC makers and chipmakers to optimize how much memory a PC needs to reserve for its hardware, enabling more for Windows.

articles.title: Google’s Gemini-powered Home Speaker is already on sale for 20 percent off
articles.summary: The Google Home Speaker is on sale for $79.99 ($20 off) at multiple retailers, marking the Gemini-powered smart speaker’s lowest price yet.
articles.body: If you’re looking for a good smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker is down to around $79 ($20 off) in all four colors at Best Buy, Walmart, and Target. That’s the best price we’ve seen for the Gemini-powered speaker, which launched in June and represents Google’s first smart speaker in several years. [Product: Google Home Speaker | In her review, my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy noted that Google’s new Home Speaker offers a nice balance of sound quality, size, and design. It’s smaller than the prior-gen Nest Audio, making it easy to place anywhere in your home. However, despite its small size, it produces loud, clear audio with 360-degree sound. Our own David Pierce even found it sounded cleaner, louder, and sharper than Amazon’s similarly priced Echo Dot Max, though Tuohy preferred the latter’s fuller sound and stronger bass. The older Nest Audio still sounds better overall, but Google’s latest speaker takes up less space and costs slightly less. The Google Home Speaker also offers a few useful smart home upgrades. It supports Matter and includes a Thread border router, allowing you to connect and control a wide range of compatible smart home devices. It’s also the first Google smart speaker that can double as an audio output for the Google TV Streamer 4K, letting you play TV audio through one or two speakers instead of your TV’s built-in speakers. Tuohy found it worked well and delivered clear dialogue, though sound quality varied depending on what she was watching. One of its most notable features is support for Gemini, which is also available on older Google speakers and is much better at understanding natural language and complex requests than the old Google Assistant. In her testing, Tuohy found it could handle multiple smart home commands at once and respond to conversational requests, like turning down the air conditioner when she mentioned feeling too hot. It’s also particularly impressive at answering general knowledge questions, though it can be slow and unreliable at times. Keep in mind, too, that some features require a $10-a-month Google Home Premium subscription, including Gemini Live, which lets you have extended conversations with the assistant without repeating the wake word. articles.title: Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
articles.summary: Apple’s new watchOS beta includes a first look at Siri Recap and Live Rewind on Apple Watch.
articles.body: Starting today, Siri can tune into the Apple Watch’s mic with Audio Intelligence features that are available in the new watchOS 27.3 developer beta rolling out now. The two new additions are Siri Recap, which uses “ambient listening” to generate summaries of your conversation, and Live Rewind, which generates text transcripts of the last 15 seconds of audio your watch’s mic detected. Apple is also releasing its redesigned Health app for testing today in the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and announced expanded language support in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese. It adds sections like a new Insights tab with summaries for heart, sleep, fitness, and other data that pop up during the day, a For You section with personalized recommendations, and health content like educational videos and articles. Apple: * Live Rewind, which can help users recall what was just said in conversation. A double-press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so the user can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with. Users can ask Siri about the content of the text or save it to the Siri app to revisit later. * Siri Recap, which can create high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment. When it comes to the implications of an ambient, always-listening AI, Apple has released this Audio Intelligence Privacy Overview (pdf) about how it plans to protect users’ privacy when their watch is listening around the clock. It goes into detail about Apple’s claims that users’ raw audio “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.” According to Apple, “If you use iCloud with two-factor authentication and have a device passcode, any Siri Recap summary or Live Rewind text snippet you choose to save syncs across your devices end-to-end encrypted in the Siri app.”

articles.title: You can’t hit a wrong note when playing along with songs on Casio’s new keyboard
articles.summary: The $400 CT-FS1 features Casio’s Feel Sync technology that helps inexperienced musicians hit only the right notes.
articles.body: Casio announced a new addition to its Casiotone line of portable electronic keyboards with a feature that could help aspiring musicians master skills like rhythm and timing without the frustrations or discouragement of hitting the wrong note. The Casiotone CT-FS1 is available now for $399.99 in a monochromatic black or white version where even the 61 touch-responsive keys are all the same color. It can run on AA batteries or a power adapter but at just under 10 pounds in weight it’s definitely not the smallest of portable keyboards. There’s built-in stereo speakers and Bluetooth connectivity if you’re playing for others, as well as a physical headphone jack. [Image: The keyboard is available in a monochromatic midnight black or alpine white color scheme. The keyboard’s most compelling feature is what Casio calls its Feel Sync technology that works alongside a new Feel Sync mobile app available for iOS and Android devices. Through the app you can import a song file which is analyzed by an algorithm before playing through the keyboard. As you play along with the song the keyboard will only produce notes that match the song’s harmony, no matter what keys you press. You’re still responsible for timing and matching the song’s rhythm, but the keyboard takes care of everything else so you can work on developing your creative expression without being self-conscious about it sounding awful. [Product: Casiotone CT-FS1 | The CT-FS1 can be played like a standard keyboard without the Feel Sync assistance, but because it’s long enough to accommodate two musicians, you can also split the keyboard into two zones. One side works like a traditional keyboard for an experienced musician to play, while the other benefits from the real time Feel Sync corrections.

articles.title: Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
articles.summary: Here are a few first impressions of the Siri Recap and Live Rewind Audio Intelligence features that arrived today in the watchOS 27.3 developer beta.
articles.body: It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge. That said, here are some initial impressions. What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review.) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public. The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone. [Image: The onboarding process is quite clear. Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap on only at the office during weekdays from 1PM to 4PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.) Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two. [Image: [Image: [Image: I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had many organic, lengthy spoken conversations yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a sense for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims. My first Siri Recap was for an editorial planning meeting for a story I’m working on. It was decent at identifying different topics discussed, and I was impressed that it stripped out some sensitive information. Any outsider looking at these notes would be terribly confused. Ironically, it meant that this summary wasn’t the most useful for my job. What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Apple’s said publicly that Siri Recap is meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. That rings true based on my first one. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations. In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.

articles.title: Delnaaz Irani: Rejection isn’t a statement on your worth as an actor; adaptability is key to longevity
articles.summary: At a time when many seasoned actors struggle to find work, Delnaaz Irani has continued to remain active across mediums, from theatre, films and television
articles.body: At a time when many seasoned actors struggle to find work, Delnaaz Irani has continued to remain active across mediums, from theatre, films and television to now OTT. Along the way, she has also moved beyond the comic roles that once defined her screen image, taking on characters that showcase a different side of her as an actor.Having spent nearly three decades in the industry, Delnaaz attributes her longevity to her willingness to work across mediums and her professionalism. She says, “I never looked at a medium as ‘too small’. My advice to actors who are struggling today is simple: don’t sit at home waiting for that one ‘perfect’ role. If you aren’t getting a massive project, do theatre, short films or create your own space on digital platforms. Most importantly, don’t take rejection personally. A rejection isn’t a statement on your worth as an actor; it’s just a casting mismatch. Keep reinventing your skills, stay visible and treat everyone on set with respect because longevity is built on reputation.”Delnaaz has also been careful about the kinds of roles she accepts as she grows older, particularly when it comes to being cast as a mother or grandmother. For her, age should not determine the scope of a character. She says, “It is definitely a conscious effort, and I won’t deny that it takes a lot of courage to say no. In our industry, the moment you cross a certain age or phase, writers immediately want to push you into the background as a generic parental figure or a grandmother. Whenever a role feels like it is designed merely to age me on screen without adding any depth to the story, I politely step away. It is about setting boundaries. If you accept a poorly sketched older stereotype just for the sake of working, the industry stamps that label on you. I’d rather wait for a role that celebrates my spirit than one that merely counts my years.”Moving beyond comedy was another challenge. After being identified with bubbly characters such as Sweetu in Kal Ho Naa Ho and Kavita in Yes Boss, she had to convince filmmakers that she could take on more varied roles. She says, “It was an incredibly challenging journey because when you do comedy well, the industry assumes that is the only thing you can do. For years, every script that came my way felt like a variation of Sweetu from Kal Ho Naa Ho or Kavita from Yess Boss. While I am endlessly grateful for the love those roles brought me, I eventually started feeling restricted as an artiste. Breaking out required a significant shift. I had to start turning down steady paychecks. Turning down roles that followed the same template was terrifying because you worry people will think you are being difficult or arrogant. But I had to take that risk to convince filmmakers to see me differently. It took time, long conversations with casting directors and a lot of patience. I had to tell them, ‘Give me an audition for a serious character and let me show you what else I can do.’ The journey taught me that you cannot blame the industry for typecasting you if you keep accepting the same kinds of roles.”Adaptability has also helped Delnaaz navigate an industry where audience preferences and platforms continue to evolve. From television to reality shows and now streaming projects, she has made a conscious effort to keep pace with changing formats. “I think staying relevant comes down to a balance of 80 per cent adaptability and 20 per cent gratitude for good timing. I have never allowed myself to become a relic of the past. You cannot be rigid in this business. If you hold on to ‘how things used to be in the 90s’, the industry and the audience will leave you behind.”‘OTT satisfies the artiste in me who craves detail’Her recent OTT outing with Chumbak offered a different working experience from daily television, particularly in terms of preparation and the time available to develop a character. She says, “The biggest difference between television and a streaming project is the luxury of time and having bound scripts. In daily television, you are constantly racing against a telecast deadline, whereas on an OTT set, you know the exact arc of your character from start to finish before the first camera rolls. There is room to breathe, rehearse and perfect the nuances with creators like Aatish Kapadia and JD Majethia. OTT satisfies the artiste in me who craves detail, while television keeps me connected to the grassroots audience that has sustained me for decades.”Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. articles.body: Apple has finally given the MacBook Pro something many people have wanted for years: a touchscreen. The company unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pro on Oct. 28, introducing a new way to interact with its laptop. It also brings a stunning OLED display, a thinner design and some serious processing power. However, there's one detail that might make you think twice before reaching for your wallet. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro starts at $2,899. That's a lot of money for a laptop, even by Apple's standards. So, what exactly are you getting for that price? More importantly, will touching your MacBook's screen make enough of a difference to justify an upgrade? Let's look at what Apple has introduced and who might benefit most. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. 8 BIGGEST THINGS WE LEARNED FROM APPLE'S 2026 EVENT Apple finally brings touch to the MacBook Pro For years, Apple maintained that the Mac worked best with a keyboard and trackpad. Meanwhile, Windows laptop owners have enjoyed touchscreen options for a long time. Apple even experimented with touch controls through its Touch Bar, but that feature never replaced the traditional laptop experience. Now Apple has changed course. Its new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lets you interact directly with the screen. You can scroll through websites with your finger or pinch to zoom into photos. Apple also lets you drag content between windows and interact with supported creative apps. Think about how often you instinctively touch your laptop screen, especially after spending years using an iPhone or iPad. Now that gesture will actually do something on the new MacBook Pro. Apple also redesigned the hinge to keep the display steadier when you touch it. That's a thoughtful addition because nobody wants a screen wobbling every time they tap a button. However, this remains a traditional laptop. It doesn't fold into a tablet, and it doesn't support Apple Pencil. You'll still use the keyboard and trackpad for much of your work. That may disappoint anyone hoping to replace both a MacBook and an iPad with one device. The OLED display could be the bigger story While everyone is talking about the touchscreen, Apple's new display technology might have an even greater impact on your everyday experience. The company calls it the PROLED XDR Display, and it uses tandem OLED technology. Unlike traditional laptop screens that rely on a backlight, OLED pixels produce their own light. That allows the display to show deep blacks alongside bright highlights without the same backlight glow. Apple says the new screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness for both HDR and SDR content. It also delivers a claimed 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio and supports refresh rates up to 120Hz for smoother motion. Those numbers sound impressive, but what will you actually notice? Photos should look more vibrant, especially when you're viewing pictures taken on your iPhone. Movies can show more detail in dark scenes. If you edit videos or work with photography, the improved color accuracy could be especially useful. Apple has also added an antireflective coating to help reduce glare. An optional nano-texture finish provides additional reflection control for people who work in bright environments. For someone who spends hours looking at a laptop screen, these improvements could be more valuable than touch alone. A touchscreen MacBook Pro with serious processing power Apple isn't holding back on performance. The new touchscreen MacBook Pro comes with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max processor. Both target people who need more processing power than a basic laptop typically provides. If you're editing high-resolution video or working with large photo libraries, these chips are designed to handle that workload. Apple also offers configurations with up to 128GB of unified memory and 16TB of storage. However, those upgrades can drive the price considerably higher. The new MacBook Pro runs macOS 27 and includes Apple Intelligence alongside Apple's upgraded Siri AI. It also brings Dynamic Island to the Mac for the first time. That familiar feature from the iPhone sits near the top of the display and gives you access to live updates and useful controls. For video calls, Apple includes a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera. Meanwhile, an upgraded six-speaker system promises deeper bass. The laptop also includes Thunderbolt 5 connectivity and an HDMI port, which should appeal to people connecting external displays. 12 BIGGEST APPLE WWDC 2026 TAKEAWAYS YOU NEED TO KNOW Apple's new MacBook Pro is thinner and lighter One concern with touchscreen laptops is whether all that additional technology makes them heavier. Apple says it has managed to move in the opposite direction. The new 14-inch touchscreen MacBook Pro weighs about three pounds, roughly half a pound less than its predecessor. The 16-inch model comes in at four pounds, approximately 0.7 pounds lighter. Both models also feature slimmer designs. That should make carrying a MacBook Pro between meetings or packing one for a trip a little easier. Apple promises up to 24 hours of battery life, depending on the configuration and usage. That's an impressive claim for a machine with this much performance and such a bright display. However, we'll need independent testing to see how battery life holds up during real-world work. How much does Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro cost? Apple has positioned its touchscreen MacBook Pro firmly in premium territory. The 14-inch model with the M5 Pro chip starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch version starts at $3,399. If you want the more powerful M5 Max processor, prices jump to $4,499 for the 14-inch model and $4,799 for the 16-inch version. And remember, those are starting prices for each configuration. Adding more memory or storage can increase the total substantially. There is another important detail. Apple introduced a separate 14-inch MacBook Pro with its newer M6 chip on Oct. 27. That model starts at $1,999, but it uses a Liquid Retina XDR Display without touch support. That means you're looking at a $900 difference between Apple's entry-level M6 MacBook Pro and its least expensive touchscreen model. Of course, the more expensive version also includes an M5 Pro processor and the upgraded OLED display. These are different performance configurations, so the additional $900 doesn't represent the cost of touch alone. For another perspective, the previous 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M5 Pro chip started at $2,499. That makes the new touchscreen version $400 more expensive than its comparable predecessor. Still, this gives you a meaningful choice. You can buy a powerful new MacBook Pro for considerably less if you don't need to interact directly with the screen. We've previously reported on how rising AI chip costs have pushed Apple prices higher. This latest introduction adds another premium option to an already expensive lineup. Will your favorite Mac apps work with touch? Apple says many existing Mac apps will respond to touch immediately because macOS can translate finger taps into mouse clicks. That should make basic interaction straightforward, even before developers fully optimize their software. However, Apple's bigger ambition involves creative applications. The company demonstrated touch controls in Final Cut Pro that let editors manipulate clips directly on the screen. Musicians can use Logic Pro to play virtual instruments with their fingers. Apple also expects third-party apps, including Adobe Lightroom and Microsoft Office applications, to take advantage of the new touch capabilities. That sounds promising. Still, a touchscreen doesn't automatically make every app easier to use. Tiny buttons and crowded menus can be frustrating when you're trying to select something precisely with a finger. Early hands-on reports suggest that touch works smoothly for common gestures. However, some smaller macOS controls can still be awkward to tap. Those are preliminary impressions rather than findings from extended testing. It will be interesting to see how quickly developers adapt their interfaces and whether people continue using touch regularly after the initial excitement wears off. Should you upgrade to Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro? This is the question I'd ask before spending nearly $3,000. If you already own a relatively recent MacBook Pro that handles everything you throw at it, I wouldn't rush to replace it solely for touchscreen capabilities. A mouse or trackpad still gives you excellent control, especially when you're working on detailed projects. However, if you edit video professionally or spend your days working with photos, the OLED display could make a real difference. The improved portability also makes the new model appealing to people who regularly travel with demanding workloads. For everyday activities like email and web browsing, a less expensive MacBook Air or standard MacBook Pro will probably be more than enough. Before making that decision, take a look at our guide explaining how to know when it's time to replace your Mac. A computer that still performs well may have several good years left. You can also explore our best laptops for 2026 at CyberGuy.com to compare other options before committing to Apple's premium model. One more suggestion: If you're considering the touchscreen MacBook Pro, visit an Apple Store when it becomes available on Nov. 6. Spend some time using the touchscreen alongside the keyboard and trackpad. That hands-on experience could tell you more than any specification sheet. Pro tip: Don't forget to protect your new MacBook If you're spending nearly $3,000 on a new MacBook Pro, protecting that investment should be a priority. While macOS includes built-in security features, Macs can still face malicious downloads and online scams. I recommend keeping your software updated and using strong antivirus software for an additional layer of protection. Strong antivirus software can help detect malware and warn you about dangerous websites before they cause trouble. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. Kurt's key takeaways I have to give Apple credit for finally bringing a touchscreen to the MacBook Pro. It feels like a feature that should have arrived years ago, especially when we're all so accustomed to touching the screens on our phones and tablets. I'm also impressed by what Apple is promising with its new OLED display. For people who work with visual content, that could be the most compelling reason to upgrade. But here's where I hesitate. At $2,899, Apple is asking a lot for a feature that many competing laptops have offered for years. And with the standard M6 MacBook Pro starting at $1,999, there's a pretty compelling argument for saving that extra $900. I want to see how useful touch becomes in everyday work before calling this a must-have upgrade. My advice is to try it in person before spending the money. A touchscreen sounds great, but the real test is whether you still reach for it after the excitement wears off. Would you pay nearly $3,000 for a touchscreen MacBook Pro? articles.title: Does opting out of TV tracking work?
articles.summary: A new study from Northeastern University shows that while most TV operating systems respect ACR opt-outs, not all do.﻿
articles.body: The fact our TVs are gathering our information isn’t new, but what and how they’re tracking — and if we can stop it — is hard to figure out. Researchers at Northeastern University monitored 12 TVs from 10 manufacturers to test whether opting out of automatic content recognition (ACR) actually works. While opting out was effective for most TVs — including LG, Amazon Fire TV, a Sony Bravia running Google TV, and those with Vidaa OS (which can be found on TVs from Hisense, Toshiba, and smaller brands like the Supersonic used in the study) — Samsung and Roku kept sending some data. And Walmart’s Vizio TV continued on as if the opt-out hadn’t even happened. ACR systems sample the audio or video playing on a TV, convert them into digital fingerprints, and send them to a database to identify what’s being watched. TV companies use that information to make recommendations of what to watch next, provide viewing metrics, and allow for targeted ads. The researchers wanted to understand when ACR was running on each TV, whether opting out did anything, and what type of data ACR systems were capturing. Because there are many different TV operating systems, and manufacturers keep smart TVs locked down, ACR activity needs to be inferred based on where the TV sends data. --- TVs used in the study Samsung QN32Q60DAF — Tizen OS LG TV 32LR655BPUA — webOS Roku TV 32R3B5 — Roku OS TCL TV 32S350R — Roku OS Sony K-43S20M2 — Google TV OS Vizio VHD32M-0810 — Vizio OS Fire TV HD32N200A — Fire OS Supersonic SC-1520VTV — Vidaa OS Westinghouse WX24HX2800 — Xumo OS Hisense 32A4K (with no ACR) — Google TV OS TCL 32S250G (with no ACR) — Google TV OS Sony KD32W830K (with no ACR) — Google TV OS --- To answer those questions, the team developed a suite of automated experiments across all the TV operating systems. They used Northeastern’s Mon(IoT)r software and SPHERE Research Infrastructure testbeds to capture and analyze all network traffic from each TV, which let them determine when ACR tracking was active and figure out where the TVs were likely sending that data. They played content on each TV from first-party streaming services such as LG Channels and The Roku Channel; third-party streaming like Netflix and YouTube; over an HDMI cable; using the over-the-air antenna; and via screen mirroring, all to see if there was any difference in ACR traffic on different inputs. They found that several of the TVs tested didn’t seem to have any ACR activity whatsoever, including a Westinghouse Xumo TV and three TVs from Sony, Hisense, and TCL running Google TV OS. (Another Sony TV with Google TV did have ACR enabled.) Of the TVs with ACR-associated network traffic, all of them scan over-the-air transmissions, while everyone but Google and Amazon uses it on first-party streaming services (such as The Roku Channel and LG Channels). Third-party apps like Netflix and YouTube? No ACR except a small amount on webOS, which disappears when opted out. Screen mirroring also looks to be safe from monitoring on all TVs but the one running Vidaa OS. To figure out whether each OS used audio or video fingerprinting, the experimenters played content that had both video and audio, just audio with a black screen, and just video with no audio, and watched for changes in network traffic to the ACR endpoints. They found that Tizen likely uses video fingerprinting, webOS and Vidaa use audio, and Fire TV OS, Google TV OS, Roku OS, and Vizio OS use a combination of both. Ideally, opting out of ACR activity should stop all data transmission to suspected ACR endpoints, and for webOS, Fire OS, Vidaa OS, and the Sony Google TV, that’s what happened. But it wasn’t always the case. Samsung’s Tizen OS activity decreased, but not completely, with ACR-correlated traffic still showing while using the antenna, first-party streaming, and HDMI. And on the two Roku OS TVs (one from TCL and one from Roku), ACR still applied to the Roku Channel app. TCL discloses this limitation in menu settings, while the Roku TV does not. Opting out on the Vizio TV didn’t change ACR-correlated traffic at all. (Vizio settled a lawsuit with the FTC in 2017 related to consumer data gathering.) I reached out to Walmart for comment about the Vizio TV’s performance in the study but did not hear back before press time. As the paper notes, because almost all network traffic sent from the TVs to the suspected ACR endpoints was encrypted, the researchers couldn’t be entirely sure that the traffic that remained after opting out was ACR traffic. “We interpret the continued presence of traffic consistent with ACR tracking after opt-out as suspicious, though we cannot confirm the contents of the network traffic (due to encryption), nor whether data is processed or retained on the server side.” It doesn’t seem to matter if you opt out during the setup process or later down the line. “For the large-scale automated tests, we applied the opt-out through the TVs’ settings menus after setup, not during the setup process,” project lead professor David Choffnes told The Verge via email. But the researchers “also manually tested certain TVs (the Vizio TV and the Fire TV) after a factory reset, and the results were unchanged,” he told me. The testing order was also randomized to prevent earlier experiments from influencing later ones. [Image: TVs primarily track data over the antenna, HDMI, and with first-party streaming services such as The Roku Channel on a Roku TV. Disturbingly, during the study, the researchers discovered a vulnerability with Vidaa OS exposing unencrypted information. Because of the vulnerability, the researchers were able to access an MQTT broker — an intermediary between Vidaa OS and Unruly, a video ad platform — and receive ACR results from other Vidaa TV users. > “Each message carries a Client ID, a permanent identifier for the TV that can’t be reset, along with the time zone, the app name, the input (antenna, HDMI), the antenna channel and an audio fingerprint.” Over a period of three hours, they collected data from over 1 million unique TVs. They informed Vidaa of the vulnerability, which the company confirmed and has since addressed by requiring a login for the server (although messages are still sent unencrypted). [Image: After opting out of ACR, tracking stopped on most TVs, but some traffic was still detected with Tizen OS, Roku OS, and especially Vizio OS. The paper recommends ways to protect ourselves from TVs harvesting our data. The easiest is to disconnect your TV from the internet, both wired and wireless, and instead use a streaming device that doesn’t run ACR. If you want to continue using the built-in apps, they suggest using webOS, Fire TV OS, Google TV on Sony, and Vidaa OS — just make sure to opt out of everything you can. They also provide a blocklist of endpoints you can restrict using blockers like Pi-hole that don’t break the TVs or affect view quality. The researchers call on TV makers to make changes, including listing every input that ACR watches and putting that information in the privacy policy (some companies do this more clearly than others), and to authenticate and encrypt all ACR traffic. And they say regulators need to hold manufacturers to task and make sure opt-out agreements work fully to protect us. I agree that there needs to be more transparency from TV manufacturers about ACR and, more broadly, what data of ours they collect and when. The Northeastern study helps to pinpoint when data is gathered, but there’s still a lot that’s seemingly intentionally hidden. And it shouldn’t be up to independent researchers to discover and disclose any of this. It should be the responsibility of the companies doing the collecting. It’s time for them to stop hiding what they’re doing.

articles.title: Bluetooth is getting a big boost to data transfer speeds
articles.summary: The Bluetooth SIG has officially adopted a new feature called High Data Throughput that increases the speed and bandwidth of the popular wireless format.
articles.body: The Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) that oversees the wireless standard has formally adopted Bluetooth High Data Throughput (HDT) as an optional feature of the Bluetooth Core 7.0. It’s an upgrade the Bluetooth SIG has been previewing over the past year that increases Bluetooth LE’s maximum supported bit rate from 2 Mbps to 7.5 Mbps. It will allow for higher resolution audio to be streamed but also improvements to battery life and reliability. The primary application for Bluetooth HDT will once again be for wireless audio, with the first devices supporting the new feature expected to appear sometime in 2027. The increased bit rate will support high-resolution audio but also new wireless audio experiences including spatial audio and multi-channel surround sound without requiring proprietary wireless formats. [Image: The Bluetooth SIG has been demonstrating the Bluetooth HDT upgrades over the past year. Bluetooth HDT will benefit other wireless devices beyond headphones. Smartwatches could sync more training, health, and fitness data to a phone without a reduction in battery life because HDT can transfer more data in less time, requiring the Bluetooth radio to be on for shorter periods. Spatial computing and extended reality devices could offer more robust experiences without needing a connection to Wi-Fi, and HDT will benefit the ever-growing number of personal AI devices, allowing them to more efficiently hand off data to be processed by a smartphone so they can be lighter and smaller. Even the simple act of updating the firmware on a smartwatch or smart home accessories could feel faster and become a task that doesn’t need to be put off until later when you’re not using your device. “Bluetooth HDT brings a new level of performance to Bluetooth technology, expanding the role it can play across consumer, commercial, and industrial markets and creating a powerful foundation for the next generation of wireless innovation,” said Neville Meijers, CEO of the Bluetooth SIG. “As the world’s most widely used wireless standard, Bluetooth technology has continually evolved to meet the growing demands of an increasingly connected world.”

articles.title: Stunt Coordinator Geeta Tandon calls out disrespect on Anil Kapoor's show India Ke Top 1%; Actor reacts to her allegations
articles.summary: Stunt coordinator Geeta Tandon has accused the team of Anil Kapoor's show India Ke Top 1% of disrespect.
articles.body: Stunt coordinator Geeta Tandon has accused the team of Anil Kapoor's show India Ke Top 1% of disrespect. She claimed that she and her son were invited as guests for an upcoming episode but waited for nine hours, with no clear update from the production team. 3. She also alleged that the production manager was dismissive when she asked why they were being made to wait.Geeta took to her social media account to share an eight-slide post in which she mentioned about being invited as a guest on the show along with her son. She further said that she joined the show without payment for exposure but felt disrespected by how things were handled.The former Khatron Ke Khiladi contestant revealed she and her son arrived on the set at 12:30 pm. They were then informed that the segment would be shot in a few hours. According to Geeta, they waited for almost nine hours without being informed about the delay. They were made to wait inside a tent with no proper explanation from the production team.She also revealed that she kept asking the non-fiction show's team for updates but was not given any proper information. "I gave up a day's work and even called my son back from Goa specifically for the shoot," she wrote.Geeta shared that she confronted the team over the long wait and their behaviour. She wrote in her post that the production manager, Jaydeep, responded, "If they want to leave, let them leave. But they can't leave without signing."This did not go well with Geeta, who asked the show's team why she and her son were not allowed to leave without signing a document. Geeta said she refused to accept their behaviour and added that they left the set at 9:15 pm after waiting for nearly nine hours."I did not come there asking for a favour. Your team invited me. Your team repeatedly followed up with me. I gave you my time, my professional commitments and my son's time, without asking for a single rupee. The least I expected was basic human dignity," she wrote.She tagged the production house, host Anil Kapoor and special guest for the episode Farah Khan, informing them about the mismanagement. However, she set the record straight that she doesn't blame the actor or the filmmaker for personally instructing the team to treat her that way. She just wanted to inform them about her experience on the sets.She said, "Being a celebrity should not determine how much respect someone deserves. The person standing behind the camera deserves the same dignity as the person standing in front of it."Farah Khan and Anil Kapoor respond to Geeta's postFarah Khan replied to Geeta's post and apologised for the incident. She said she was unaware that Geeta was waiting on the set, as she was busy shooting the second episode in the evening. Farah commented on her post, "Geetaji apologies.. I had no idea you were there as I was shooting for the 2nd episode in the evening.. otherwise would have made you sit in my van. As would Anil if he knew.. we have tremendous respect for you and your hard work."Anil Kapoor also reacted to the stunt coordinator's post. He said he was sorry to hear about her experience and the way she and her son were treated. "Geeta ji, it genuinely saddens me to hear this. As the host, I always wanted everyone who was part of the show to feel welcome and respected. You and your son came as our guests. I'm sorry that your experience left you feeling otherwise," he wrote.Anil Kapoor also mentioned in the comment that her feedback mattered to him and that respect should be given to everyone in the industry. Geeta thanked the actor for his response and hoped others would not face the same situation.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Rian Johnson explains why he had to build his own iPhone camera app
articles.summary: Chromagraph Camera lets anyone with an iPhone get the look used by the director of Knives Out and The Last Jedi.
articles.body: Rian Johnson is an analog photography devotee. The director of Knives Out and The Last Jedi can often be spotted on set with a Leica M6 at his side, documenting production on film. But sometimes, it’s still easier to reach for a phone. So Johnson started wondering if the photos from his iPhone could be made to look more like the grade he applies to his movies. The result is Chromagraph Camera, a $13 iOS app that bypasses elements of Apple’s image processing pipeline and applies the same look used on Johnson’s movies. The app, made by Johnson and his longtime cinematographer, Steve Yedlin, is shockingly simple, with just a few primary settings, but it gives anyone who buys it access to image processing decisions good enough for a Hollywood production. “The reality is, as much as I love my Leica, as much as I love my other gear, it’s a pain in the butt having a camera on your shoulder, or a massive backpack with four cameras in it,” Johnson says. “And I always have my phone with me.” [Media: Watch | Listen | Get ad-free Johnson has been tinkering with phone photography for a long time. Back before the smartphone days, he bought a Nokia phone with a proper camera — at least, proper for the time. “It was like the first one where they advertised the camera on it as the main feature of it,” he says. “And it was garbage, the camera was awful, but it took these photos that were grainy and contrasty and funky and beautiful.” Smartphone photography has progressed substantially since then, but that progression has also come with a loss of character. The default photos coming out of modern phones tend to look sharper, brighter, and more clinical than in the days before computational photography took hold. You can work around this, but it generally means shooting RAW and editing the images yourself. [Image: [Image: Initially, Johnson tried shooting with the iPhone’s default camera and editing in Snapseed to get his desired look. He then graduated to third-party RAW camera apps, only to get bogged down shuffling files back and forth and tweaking endless sliders. “I would do a lot of messing with every photo,” he says, “and then it was a little like I’d wandered through the woods and I wasn’t sure how I’d gotten there.” Smartphone makers have started including tools to add more character to their images. Apple added a texture panel with film, grain, and halation settings to the iPhone 18 Pro, and Google put a new “Camera Looks” panel in the Pixel 11. But these still don’t afford the level of control you get from starting with a RAW image. And if you really want to dial in a look that feels unique to you, that’s what you need to start with. Yedlin is convinced that given the right set of algorithms and settings, there is no perceivable difference between an image shot on film and one shot on digital. A few years back, he set out to make a series of color grading scripts to give Johnson’s movies the organic look of celluloid. Eventually, those tools allowed Johnson to apply their movie color pipeline to his still RAW files and film scans. That gave Johnson the confidence to bring the same ideas to mobile. [Image: [Image: “I knew he could do it,” Johnson says. “I called Steve up and bullied him ... I kept saying, ‘Can we do it for iPhone photos?’” Chromagraph Camera is a camera, of course, with settings for maximum exposure time, burst mode, and color tuning, but maybe one of the most fun things to do is to import RAW images you’ve already shot and process them in the app. It’s a camera and editor in one, but I’ve found myself importing old RAWs and seeing what Yedlin’s film-like processing does to my existing library. It doesn’t work for every photo right out of the gate, but after import you’ll have tons of options for tuning, like tone, color, saturation, and texture. [Image: [Image: Johnson’s app is clearly still in its early stages, with settings and UI elements laid out in sometimes unexpected places. But the core of the app, the processing, is what is drawing people toward it. Over the weekend, Chromagraph went viral on social media, with many early users marveling at the app’s results compared to Apple’s defaults. Even though this app gives Johnson what he’s been craving with smartphone photography, he remains entranced by much earlier photographic techniques. While chatting with me over coffee, I saw his eyes light up when he started talking about the 8 x 10 wet plate photography he’s been experimenting with at home. He even recently set up his own darkroom and continues to experiment with the chaotic, exciting art of analog photography. “It’s like nerd fishing,” he says. “It’s about the actual process of doing it for me.” Photography by David Imel / The Verge

articles.title: Anker’s new window-mounted camera monitors the outside of your home from within it
articles.summary: Anker’s new Eufy Window Camera E10 sticks to the inside of an outward-facing window so it can watch your yard or driveway without being exposed to the elements.
articles.body: Anker announced a new indoor security camera that’s designed to watch your yard, driveway, or front porch through a window, instead of monitoring what’s inside your home. The new Anker Eufy Window Camera E10 takes a similar approach to the Wyze Window Cam that launched nearly a year ago. It installs right against a window using an including mounting sticker to reduce glare and reflections, but the camera doesn’t require any weatherproofing since it’s not enduring the elements outdoors. The Eufy Window Camera E10 is available now for $79.99 through Anker’s online store and Amazon, making it more than twice as expensive as the $34.98 Wyze Window Cam. But the E10 comes with a few useful upgrades. Wyze’s camera is limited to 1080p, while the E10 has a much higher maximum resolution of 2.5K, capturing more detailed 15fps videos at 2,688 x 1,520. articles.title: I tried Apple's Siri Recaps. They're surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple's AI-powered Siri Recaps won me over in just one day, despite my privacy reservations. But there's still room for improvement.
articles.body:
On Tuesday, Apple rolled out a potentially controversial set of Audio Intelligence features into testing with the first developer beta versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The betas bring four new AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.

After just a day with Apple’s Siri Recaps feature on my Apple Watch, I can already see how its value may ultimately outweigh any creepiness factor that comes from the AI-powered audio recording and summarization it provides. However, I also see areas where AI-assisted note-taking can go too far, capturing things that aren’t worth remembering, and where there’s room for improvement.

The first two, sound and song detection, don’t represent potential privacy concerns; they are designed to detect either important sounds — like an alarm or doorbell — or identify a song using Shazam’s technology. The former helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users navigate the world, and the latter is something we’ve already done with our iPhone for nearly two decades now.

It’s the two other features, Live Rewind and Siri Recaps, that have raised concerns. The features record and then transcribe or summarize the conversations happening with and around the Apple Watch’s owner. Live Rewind lets you go back to see what was said in the past 15 seconds, while Siri Recaps summarize audio throughout your day, saving notes of the important things that were said.

Apple has taken care to ensure the privacy of these AI features by processing the audio and running AI models on-device, when possible, and by not identifying speakers, storing raw audio files, and redacting private information, like government ID numbers or personal account information.

Still, some are put off by the idea that we’re now normalizing the idea that technology is always listening .

I find myself sympathizing with both camps. I often lament that we’ve allowed technology to become so pervasive in our daily lives, but I still see the value in what Apple has built.

I haven’t yet had an appropriate time to test Live Rewind, nor do I think this will be a feature I use as often. I’m more likely to say “sorry, what?” or “can you repeat that?” if I missed something that was said, before turning to my Apple Watch for help.

But with Siri Recaps, I immediately saw how this could become a feature I rely on regularly to save important notes for later.

I was able to test the feature in a real-world scenario yesterday, when we were dropping off my teen’s car for repairs and picking up a rental. At both places, employees shared a lot of information about time frames, prices, and policies that were delivered verbally. The information came too fast to stop and write anything down. Yet when I returned to Siri Recaps later in the day, it had captured key details that I may need to refer back to.

For instance, it noted the deductible, the repair time frame, the amount of gas we had in the rental at the start, and other things I wanted to remember.

One complaint is that Siri Recaps had mixed this information with other topics that were later discussed in the home, like an errand we needed to run and what time babysitting was this week, something we were discussing in order to create an appointment on the family calendar with an appropriate alert time frame.

I think these items should have been saved in a separate note titled “family schedule and errands,” rather than in the same note with the car repairs, but under a separate heading.

Because I configured Siri Recaps to run at all times, it also captured non-essential things, like our “plan” to watch the midterms coverage on TV, which is not the kind of thing you’d normally jot down a note about. It also was a stark reminder that the feature was listening in on our everyday conversations. That’s something that could feel invasive in different scenarios, if the subject being discussed was more personal in nature.

This had me considering turning off the Recap feature while at home in the evening, so family dinner table chatter doesn’t become note fodder.

While I appreciated that the Recap picked up a reminder about an errand I needed to run from one of the family conversations, other tidbits it saved — like what we were watching on TV — would only be valuable if you were exporting a Siri Recap note to Apple’s Journal app, because it was something you wanted to record for personal reasons.

I’d like to see these sorts of extraneous details saved as separate notes — or at least as dedicated sections that could be exported or deleted on their own at the end of the day.

I’d also love to be able to swipe left on an individual bullet point to remove it from the Siri Recap entirely, rather than having to enter edit mode, place the cursor, and then start deleting the text I don’t need.

Another option I’d like to have would be a setting that would allow you to automatically export any saved Siri Recap (the ones you click the bookmark icon to save) to Apple’s Notes app, instead of that being an extra step.

These Recaps could go into their own folder in the Notes app for easy reference. I can understand why this option is not the default, given how many different ways people use a general-purpose app like Notes. However, it would be useful for those of us who want to keep Notes as the central starting point for all our jotted-down reminders and to-dos.

Though I wasn’t immediately warmed up to the idea that my Watch was always listening, so to speak, I see the value of this sort of automated note-taking in daily life.
