articles.title: My therapist thinks I should chuck the Amazon Bee Frontier out a window
articles.summary: Filtering conversations and memories through AI is a reality-bending lesson in why intelligence can’t replace wisdom.
articles.body: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here. “How does that make you feel?” I get asked this a lot in therapy. Plenty of life events, big and small, have triggered this question. Three weeks ago, it was the fact that I had to ask my therapist for her consent because I was wearing the Amazon Bee Frontier during our session. That first week, I didn’t really have an answer. A lot had changed since I first tested Bee, an always-recording AI wearable, early last year. The elevator pitch is that it listens to all your conversations and uses AI to transcribe and summarize them. From there, it has a List feature that suggests to-dos, a Grow feature for identifying areas where you can improve, and various summaries that analyze the content, tone, and takeaways from your conversations. It’s even got a chatbot that can answer questions about yourself or what was said and when. In the last 19 months, it’s gotten better at distinguishing my actual speech from TV dialogue. It can now pull in information from my calendar and photos app, and suggest things to buy on Amazon based on what I’ve said. At times, particularly for job-related tasks, it’s helped me remember talking points. But most of the time, it’s led to me questioning my reality. My therapist usually lets me arrive at my own decisions, even if I often take the scenic route to the obvious conclusion. After 11 years, she’s intimately acquainted with the wackier parts of my job. But in my third week of talking about Bee, my therapist requested that I chuck this thing right out a window. [Image: It’s easy to forget this thing is recording when you’re just going about your day. It’s a bit dark, but a big reason I’m in therapy is to build trust in my own memories. I grew up with a dad who might’ve been a spy and an immigrant family that never agreed on a single version of events. Growing up, I felt unmoored. Were things truly as I’d remembered them? Were my parents the unreliable narrators, or was I? Adding in their eventual dementia to the mix made discerning truth from fiction even harder. In those moments, I had wished for a device like Bee. A reviewable record, so to speak, for moments where I wanted a sanity check. It’s funny in retrospect. Now that tech companies have started making this fantasy into a reality, what I feel is perpetually gaslit. For example, it’s disorienting to see Bee’s transcripts and summaries of my conversations, often because the AI remembers and interprets them differently than I do. Like any AI, it’s not always precise about who said what. In the past three weeks, it’s concluded that I argue with a coworker’s spouse frequently (I’ve never met them), that I think a family member has undiagnosed bipolar disorder (No one ever said that!), and that I like to put my good pants on for important video calls. (That was a joke.) Sure, it’s a relief that Bee’s newly updated transcription prowess was able to discern that I personally was not working with detectives Rust Cohle and Marty Hart to find a serial killer named the Yellow King simply because I watched True Detective. But it still doesn’t know how to handle the fact that we call my two cats Petey and Pablo various nicknames. By Bee’s estimation, I have about six additional cats named Mr. Handsome, Mr. Stylish, District Attorney Hoss, Dabah Doo Bah, Potato Demon, and Tubby McTubberson Jones. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: These mistakes are at least funny. It’s when the conversations are serious that I feel the strongest whiplash. That’s when the “improved” AI dislodges something in my brain. In my second therapy session with Bee recording, I spent the majority of the time unpacking my feelings about You Can See Everything. It’s a reality-bending movie that questions the line between truth and fiction. As much as I enjoyed the film, witnessing compulsive liars for three hours was bound to take me back to unhappier moments in my life. I should’ve turned Bee off for this session. But the truth is, I just forgot. Because the design of these devices is, in many ways, built for you to forget they’re listening. One of Bee’s capabilities is that it learns “facts” about you that you then swipe right to approve as true, or left to dismiss as false. After this session, it generated a “fact” about an instance of domestic violence I experienced as a child. This particular moment has come up multiple times in sessions over the years — revisiting it has been key to understanding and forgiving my parents, holding compassion for the circumstances that shaped them. I did not expect how awful it felt to see a traumatic event summarized so starkly in plain English. I hated having to swipe right to say, “Yes, this is true.” I didn’t expect the accompanying summary to be titled “Reclaiming Reality from Manipulative Power.” Or for it to characterize the type of person I am (deeply unsettled), the timbre of the conversation (intense, reflective, emotionally raw), or how I felt during that session (grieving, angry, and clear-eyed about manipulation). I remember that session as cathartic. There were times when I laughed or joked around. The topic was serious, yes, but I wasn’t ranting, raving, or crying. I left that session feeling light — you’d never guess that from the summary. Looking at it weeks later, I’m now wondering who’s right: me, or the AI. [Image: This device is, at times, extremely weird. I also forgot to turn Bee off during my annual physical. I was late to the appointment, and when I changed into a gown for the exam, the damn thing was just sitting in a pile of my clothes. I only realized my mistake when it was time to leave. On the one hand, it did memorialize that my doctor prescribed me Claritin for allergies and that the nurse and I talked about my dead dog Daisy. (It described me as wistful and grieving here, too, but I recall it as fond remembrance.) Ironically, it also memorialized my doctor’s feelings on AI transcription. My doctor’s AI transcription software requires patient consent and helps her with long conversations where she has to remember treatment notes. But it’s also garbage at distinguishing between two female speakers, and she spends a decent amount of time correcting it. Depending on which Bee AI template I use, it can change the summary. With the default template, the AI’s conclusions about this particular meeting include tonal analysis and takeaways. If I filter to the medical visit template, suddenly everything is much more factual. It strips away the ruminations. It’s more useful and less uncomfortable to look back on. But I also can’t help but feel that the record of what was a fairly significant healthcare appointment differs from my memory. Who is right? So, how does this all make me feel? A little bit crazy and overwhelmed. Sometimes offended. Bee has a new-ish feature called Grow. Based on your conversation history, it compiles recommendations on how you can grow as a person. It also generates suggested to-dos. To train Bee AI on my voice, during setup it asked me to describe my hobbies. I said I enjoy reading, calligraphy, cross-stitch, and running. I’ve recently gotten into fountain pens and ink swatching for journaling. You have to talk for about two minutes straight, so I ended up rambling about how I was unsure whether embroidery would be a natural progression from cross-stitch or an unnecessary side quest at this point in time. The Grow insight based on this incredibly unserious, one-sided discussion? A conversation Bee itself prompted. I dabble in too many hobbies without serious commitment. A jack of all trades, master of none. I’ve shown no progression or tangible sign of “shareable output” and should spend the next three months picking one hobby. Because I allowed Bee to integrate with my reminders list, which has an old to-read list for books I want physical copies of, it confidently stated that despite calling myself a reader, I haven’t made much progress this year. [Image: I don’t recall asking for judgement about my “serial pattern of experimentation.” Bitch, I thought, I’ve finished 39 books in 2026 so far. I’ve been practicing calligraphy and journaling for 17 years. I finished 10 cross-stitch projects this year. Most importantly, hobbies aren’t something I do for “shareable output.” I happen to firmly believe that hobbies should be exempt from cockamamie Silicon Valley-brained KPIs. Another Grow insight from some political discussion with my spouse about the midterms? “These frameworks help her contextualize current events but may also distance her from present-tense engagement; her tone in political discussion is more analytical than activist, more diagnostic than mobilized.” It then suggested that I “identify one concrete political action aligned with your values that requires less than 30 minutes and complete it this week.” In my memory, this was because we watched an episode of The Daily Show and I said, jokingly, that I was tired of US political shenanigans. Never mind my actual lived experience canvassing and as a union organizer and representative. These are just two examples. Imagine seeing some version of this every day for nearly a month. Summaries that are maybe 75 percent right, 15 percent taken out of context, and 10 percent out-of-pocket wrong. Things that are just presented to you as fact, regardless of whatever disclaimer that AI can make mistakes. You can know the truth deep in your gut and still wonder what happens when your hypervigilance slips. I said as much in my third therapy session wearing Bee. I asked my therapist to weigh in. What, I joked, did she feel watching me go through this experiment? I’ve gone through the Bee transcript of that conversation. Ironically, it didn’t summarize her thoughts on how poorly designed this device is for anxious people. I had to dig into the raw transcript to find that. According to my therapist, a device like this likely supersedes a person’s ability to trust their own instincts about what they need to do. When you outsource that, AI can generate insights that aren’t emotionally attuned and, in turn, exacerbate many of the problems a person might be trying to solve. For me, it likely triggers rumination, spiraling, and perfectionism. That’s the point where we joked that I should probably throw this thing out the window. We laughed that we’d both feel relieved when I’m not wearing this at my next session. I would say that was the most important takeaway. Bee didn’t include that in my suggested to-do list. It did, however, say this: buy nail glue, complete with a link out to Amazon.

articles.title: Apple will check shared iCloud links for ‘harmful content’
articles.summary: Apple will start checking iCloud items that are accessible to anyone who has the link for “harmful content” starting with iOS 27.3 and other 27.3 updates.
articles.body: Apple will start checking iCloud items that are accessible to anyone who has the link for “harmful content” starting with iOS 27.3 and other 27.3 updates, the company says. “When you share an item that can be accessed by Anyone with the Link in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, that content is made accessible to Apple to check for harmful content,” according to a support document reported on by 9to5Mac. Sharing something over iCloud with the “Anyone with the Link” permissions will also mean that it’s no longer end-to-end encrypted. Apple’s support document does not define what “harmful content” is. But this new approach follows calls from protestors for Apple to crack down on child sexual abuse material stored in iCloud. Apple says it “reserves the right to move, refuse, modify, remove, or delete” any harmful content that a user attempts to upload. Apple may also block or disable accounts, prevent a user from making a new account, or, “if necessary,” invoke law enforcement. The company launched the first 27.3 developer betas yesterday, and said recently it plans to launch iOS 27.3 in December.

articles.title: How I learned to love an obnoxious phone grip
articles.summary: Step away from the buttoned-up neutrals and embrace the ridiculous with a vibrant, bold phone accessory.
articles.body: Much like a great recipe, it started with a stick of butter. This wasn’t real butter; it was a friend’s new phone grip, complemented by a phone case with bold stripes. Butter is in vogue now, or at least that’s what a 12-year-old told me a few months ago. This stick of butter was labeled “unsalty” and committed to the bit by including the appropriate tablespoon markings, just like the real thing. I was enamored. “Where did you get that?” I asked. It was a PopSocket-branded combo, and I found it so irresistible I ordered an equally eye-catching grip a few weeks later. After years of carrying buttoned-up, minimalist tech, I finally said, “To hell with it. I’m gonna have some fun.” I have zero regrets, and it seems I’m not alone in this journey. Over the past few years I’ve been a vocal, occasionally regretful, member of Team No Phone Case. A case adds bulk and collects pocket lint. Why spend $800 on a piece of tech just to cover it up? If I must use a case, I want it to barely exist. This philosophy worked great with my iPhone 13 Mini, which is perfect as-is. Its size means it’s eminently grippable — no PopSocket necessary and it feels much more secure when I hold it. But phones are big now and are only getting bigger. An extended period using Google’s hefty Pixel 10 Pro Fold last year convinced me to adopt a magnetic grip just to use the thing more comfortably. At first, I gravitated toward the minimalist options like low-profile ring stands. But then I saw that stick of butter, and something clicked. A chunky grip is easy to hold. It’s fun. And since it’s just held on by a magnet, you can take it off whenever you want to present yourself as a serious grownup. Why not? I put in an order for a PopSocket shaped like a hot dog, and I was so excited when it arrived I accidentally pulled it apart. This “why not have fun” ethos has clearly been part of Bailey Hikawa’s mission for the better part of a decade. She’s been making unconventional phone grips and cases out of her Los Angeles studio since 2018. Her designs incorporate input from the disabled community, aiming to offer an easier grip for people who hold their phone differently. But they can be appreciated by anyone who’s ever felt their phone slide out of their fingers. They’re also vibrant and bold. “I would like the phone case to feel like a friend or like a new stuffed animal,” she told The Verge in 2019. Earlier this year, Apple collaborated with Hikawa on a chunky, bright MagSafe grip. Her own online shop includes other grips made of flexible, clear urethane with spaghetti noodles or baby shrimp suspended inside. They’re handmade and the very definition of one-of-a-kind. [Image: Hikawa brought her signature bold style to a recent collaboration with Apple. In more conventional territory, PopSocket has a surprising number of unusual grips and cases on offer. There’s a classic tomato pincushion, the food truck collection where I found my beloved hot dog, and an aptly named “Sugar Rush” collection. I asked PopSocket founder David Barnett whether I was alone in my pursuit of a bold grip. “We’re seeing more consumers embrace color, texture and personality in their phone accessories,” he told me over email. “I think people want their everyday essentials to feel a little less ordinary. Your phone goes everywhere with you, so why not have a little fun with it?” [Image: [Image: I think phone makers are partly to blame here, too. Aside from your stray Cosmic Orange and anything Motorola is doing, phones mostly come in shades of Boring and Light Boring. Don’t even get us started on what passes for a purple phone these days. Maybe a radical reaction to this sameness was inevitable. Whatever the reason, you can find an awful lot of punchy, vibrant grips and cases without much effort. There are color-blocked “dopamine” cases all over TikTok and Amazon, viral phone cases that hold a tube of lip gloss, and OhSnap grips in colors called things like “hazmat honey” and “electric teal.” Me and my ridiculous PopSocket are in good company. Or we will be — I left it in the office last time I was in New York and its absence has been bumming me out ever since. We’ll be reunited soon enough, but I guess if there’s one downside to being able to take a grip off your phone easily, it’s that you can accidentally leave it behind without much effort.

articles.title: Nothing CEO says company's mysterious AI-first device is dropping next month | TechCrunch
articles.summary: While it's not yet clear what kind of product the smartphone startup is cooking up, Nothing's CEO said the product is designed to leverage AI for productivity gains.
articles.body:
Nothing, the smartphone startup behind the distinctive Nothing Phone , is working on an AI product, but what it is remains unclear.

On Wednesday, CEO Carl Pei posted on X that the company’s first “AI-native product” ships in December. “It’s a tool, but one built with the personality and care that have come to define a Nothing product. It has no new screen, and it couldn’t have been an app,” Pei wrote.

Pei has teased an AI-first device for some time and the company has also said that it plans to release a pair of AI-linked smart glasses, as well as earbuds with AI integrations.

Pei’s description adds up to a screenless non-app that uses AI? He also calls it a “productivity tool.” Adding further mystique to the announcement, Pei seems to downplay any link to AI wearables.

“The whole industry is hunting for its iPhone moment: the pendant, the pin, the glasses, the companion, some magical consumer device that makes AI part of everyone’s life,” Pei wrote. “I admire the boldness, but I read this moment differently.”

No firm release date has been announced, but Nothing fans should know soon enough what the company has in store for them.

articles.summary: O Motorola Signature 27 estreia com o chip Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, acabamento em cerâmica e suporte para sete anos de atualizações do sistema Android.
articles.body:
Motorola Signature 27, novo celular topo de linha — Foto: Henrique Martin/g1

A Motorola apresentou nesta quinta (5) o Signature 27 , novo smartphone topo de linha da marca que promete uma câmera excelente, com auxílio da inteligência artificial.

O aparelho começa a ser vendido neste mês, com preços que vão de R$ 11.000 (versão com 256 GB de armazenamento) a R$ 12.000 (512 GB).

Segundo a fabricante, o aparelho tem acabamento em cerâmica, alumínio aeroespacial e materiais texturizados. O Signature 27 será vendido nas cores verde-oliva e cinza-escuro.

Motorola Signature 27 nas cores verde oliva e cinza escuro — Foto: Henrique Martin/g1

A empresa informou ainda que o Signature 27 terá sete anos de atualizações do sistema operacional Android. Nos demais celulares da marca, esse suporte costuma variar entre dois e três anos, a depender do modelo.

Na parte de câmeras, são 3 lentes na traseira:

Uma lente grande angular de 50 megapixels;

E um sensor de 200 megapixels com zoom óptico de 5x e zoom digital de até 100x.

O conjunto de câmeras fica completo com um flash LED circular e um sensor adicional para ajudar em fotos de ação/movimento, chamado Action Sensor.

O controle desse tipo de foto, como as usadas em esportes, era feito pelo software, e agora tem uma lente adicional para ajudar na estabilização da imagem.

Diz a Motorola que o Action Sensor "registra informações de movimento de forma independente das câmeras. Com o recurso Action Shot ativado, é possível congelar cenas em alta velocidade com precisão, revelando detalhes e cores".

O zoom híbrido da câmera promete melhorias na foto final com uso de processamento de imagens usando inteligência artificial .

Veja abaixo, em fotos feitas da tela do Signature 27 e a potencial mudança do que o sensor câmera "vê" (à esquerda) e o celular entrega (à direita) .

À esquerda, a tela do Signature 27 ao fotografar com zoom de 100x; à direita, a foto após processamento da imagem pelo celular — Foto: Henrique Martin/g1

A câmera frontal tem 50 megapixels de resolução.

Outro destaque do celular é a bateria de silício-carbono de 7.000 mAh . Esse tipo de tecnologia permite fabricar aparelhos mais finos e permitir maior capacidade de carga.

Concorrentes como o Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra , por exemplo, têm bateria de 5.000 mAh com tecnologia de íons de lítio.

O Signature 27 também é o primeiro smartphone da Motorola com áudio assinado pela marca dinamarquesa Bang & Olufsen (B&O).

O aparelho virá em configurações com 12 GB de memória RAM e 256 GB ou 512 GB de armazenamento interno.

Além do Signature 27, a Motorola também anunciou o smartwatch Moto Watch Ultra (R$ 4.999), com sistema WearOS, do Google, o fone de ouvido wireless Moto Buds 2 Ultra e a base de carregamento sem fios Moto Snap Wireless Charger.

Os preços dos fones e do carregador não foram divulgados.

articles.title: ‘The Pitt’ and ‘ER’ Are Similar Enough to Allow Crichton Suit, Appeals Court Rules
articles.summary: An appeals court ruled on Wednesday that “The Pitt” is similar enough to “ER” to allow Michael Crichton’s widow to pursue a lawsuit over the Emmy-winning sho...
articles.body:
An appeals court ruled on Wednesday that "The Pitt" is similar enough to "ER" to allow Michael Crichton's widow to pursue a lawsuit over the Emmy-winning show.

In a unanimous opinion, a three-judge panel denied an appeal from Warner Bros. Television, which has argued that the two shows are unrelated.

"There are clear and numerous similarities between 'The Pitt' and 'ER," the court ruled, citing the emergency room setting, the fast pace, the medical jargon, the graphic depictions of injuries, and a young, incompetent doctor fresh from medical school. "We find the details here suffice for a prima facie case."

The appeals court did dismiss a claim against key creators of the show — Noah Wyle, John Wells and R. Scott Gemmill — finding no evidence that they were aware they could be violating Crichton's contractual rights.

Crichton was a creator of "ER," which was based on a 1974 script he wrote about his experiences as a medical student. His contract with Warner Bros. Television included a "frozen rights" provision blocking the studio from making any spinoffs or reboots without his approval.

Sherri Crichton, his widow, filed the suit in August 2024, months before "The Pitt" debuted, alleging that Wells and Wyle had originally wanted to reboot "ER" and only changed course after failing to secure her permission.

Warner Bros. has argued that "The Pitt" is a completely different show, and filed a motion to throw out the suit under California's anti-SLAPP statute, which is meant to deter frivolous lawsuits that stymie free expression. Judge Wendy Chang denied the motion last year, finding that Sherri Crichton had offered enough evidence to proceed.

The appellate ruling allows the suit to move forward at the trial court. The question of whether "The Pitt" is in fact a derivative work of "ER" could ultimately be up to a jury to decide unless the parties reach a settlement before it gets to that point.

"I am deeply gratified by the Court of Appeal decision and look forward to discovery and to our case, which affects writers, creators, and their families and estates, being presented to a jury," Sherri Crichton said in a statement.

articles.title: Motorola is going ultra premium with its $1,600 ‘Signature’ phone
articles.summary: The Motorola Signature 27 comes with true flagship specs — and a sky-high price.
articles.body: Motorola is trying something it hasn’t attempted in the modern smartphone era: to make an all-out flagship slab-style phone. Previous high-end Edge devices never quite hit the mark, and lacked features that would put it in the highest flagship tiers. The company has had plenty of success with its Razr clamshell foldables, leaning on brand nostalgia and daring to make phones that actually look good. But it’s trying something different with its new Signature line, which until now hasn’t been available in the US. The Signature 27 goes a step further toward premium, daring to take on the likes of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. Motorola is leaning into a luxury aesthetic, offering a stacked feature set — with an equally luxurious $1,599 price tag. It’s a lot to ask for a starting price, but it does get you 512GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, the same as the S26 Ultra’s $1,599, 512GB variant. Samsung does offer a cheaper 256GB configuration for $1,399, though. We got our first look at the Signature 27 when Motorola previewed it earlier this year, revealing that it would use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset. The company dropped a few other details, too, like Bang & Olufsen-designed audio, 50-megapixel and 200-megapixel telephoto cameras, and two Pantone color options. Today’s full announcement fills in the gaps. It will come with a 7,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, a 6.8-inch tandem OLED screen, IP68/IP69 ratings for full dust and water resistance, and 12GB of RAM. The Signature 27 will also support the privacy-focused GrapheneOS — a first for Motorola, and for a mainstream phone sold in the US, for that matter. [Image: Motorola calls this a 1.5K “Super HD” resolution display. It’s hard to find fault with the 27’s feature set, aside from the lack of built-in Qi2 magnets, which is a bummer. The tandem OLED display uses two light-emitting panels to reach a peak brightness of 12,000 nits. The more battery efficient dual-layer might mean that the phone can reach its highest brightness setting without drawing too much power and overheating the phone, but we’ll want to see if that bears out in practice. The camera array features a 50-megapixel Sony Lytia L910 sensor with LOFIC technology, meaning it should deliver plenty of dynamic range. In addition to a 3x 200-megapixel camera and a 50-megapixel ultrawide, there’s also an Event Vision Sensor, or EVS. It’s designed to identify movement on a pixel level, which Motorola says will help “capture fast-moving subjects with greater clarity and precision.” That Bang & Olufsen audio system includes a redesigned speaker architecture for sound that’s “meant to be felt, not just heard,” according to Motorola’s press release. That’d be quite a feat to pull off with a smartphone audio system and I’m not holding my breath. Elsewhere, the Signature 27 offers up to 90W wired charging and up to 50W wireless charging — though you’ll need to use Motorola’s proprietary wireless charger. But in better news, Motorola is promising seven years of OS upgrades for the Signature 27, putting it right up there with the best support policies from Samsung and Google. [Image: [Image: Maybe it’s a case of unlucky timing that Motorola decided to go toe-to-toe with Samsung’s premium flagship just as we started gearing up for RAMageddon: Year Two. Maybe in a few years’ time every flagship phone will cost well over $1,000. But right now, $1.600 is a steep hill to ask people to climb, and the Signature 27 will need to come up with more than just an impressive spec sheet. And just to prove a point, Motorola is also announcing some updates to its wider ecosystem, too. The new Moto Watch Fit 27 claims up to 12 days of battery life, and the Moto Buds 27 offer Bose ANC with IP57 ratings for both the buds and the case. Motorola isn’t announcing pricing or an exact release date for either in the US, only that they’ll be available in the coming months. Both will arrive in the coming “weeks” in Europe and the UK, where the watch will start at £99.99 (about $134 US) and the buds will cost £179.99 (about $242). Pre-sales for the Signature 27 start on November 19th in the US; the phone goes on sale November 26th.

articles.title: The M6 MacBook Pro is probably the last of its kind
articles.summary: The design is starting to show its age next to the lighter, brighter PROLED model, but the entry-level MacBook Pro is still great.
articles.body: On November 6th, Apple will release an all-new MacBook Pro. It’s thinner and lighter and has a beautiful OLED touchscreen. It is very likely what every new MacBook Pro will look like in a couple of years. The M6 MacBook Pro, which is also out on the 6th, is not that laptop. Instead, it’s a straightforward chip bump of Apple’s entry-level MacBook Pro, in basically the same chassis Apple’s been using since 2021. Everything that was great about the M5 MacBook Pro last year, and the M4 the year before, still applies. The M6 MacBook Pro is still a great all-around computer, and a nice step up from the MacBook Air. Processor, screen, speakers, ports, power, battery life: They’re all a little better than the Air’s. The keyboard and webcam are still solid; the trackpad is still best in class. Inside the laptop, only the processor — which bumps up from a 10-core M5 to a 12-core M6 — and the N1 networking chip are new. There are just two things complicating what would otherwise be the easiest MacBook review of the year. The first is the starting price: $1,999 with 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage — the same price as the base M5 MacBook Pro since September, but up $200 since its launch a year ago. The other is the actually new MacBook Pro: the one with the OLED touchscreen. Yes, the OLED model is great. Not that someone who’s considering the base MacBook Pro should spend $900 more to get that screen today. But that design is likely to come to the entry MacBook Pro next year. The question is: Should you wait? [Product: Apple MacBook Pro 14 (2026, M6) | The entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro has only existed in its current form for two years. After the 2023 M3 model finally ditched the Touch Bar and butterfly keys, the M4 model brought it up to par with the “real” Pros, most notably by adding a third Thunderbolt port and bumping the minimum RAM from an embarrassing 8GB to a decent 16GB. The M5 version had a faster chip and double the storage speed, and that was enough to keep it among our favorite laptops. The M6 is yet another chip bump, and it adds Apple’s N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 (and also Thread, for what that’s worth.) --- Component report card * Screen: A * Webcam: A * Mic: B * Keyboard: B * Touchpad: A * Port selection: B * Speakers: A * Number of ugly stickers to remove: 0 --- The rest of the hardware is the same as it’s been for two years, which is to say it’s still great. The 14.2-inch miniLED display is bright, beautiful, and color-accurate, with 3092 x 1964 resolution and up to 1,000 nits of brightness in standard mode. The 120Hz adaptive refresh rate (which Apple calls ProMotion) really makes a difference in gaming or even just moving the cursor around. It’s the sort of thing you don’t notice when all your screens are 60Hz, but once you go higher, it’s awfully hard to go back. Of course, it’s also hard to go back from an OLED screen, like the one on the other new MacBook Pro, once you’ve used one. So it’s a good thing I haven’t used that laptop yet. The large haptic trackpad remains the best on any laptop, and the keyboard is… still fine. I have never loved Apple’s laptop keyboards, but the keys are large and well-spaced and tolerable for typing on. I’ve used worse. The speakers, on either side of the keyboard deck, are excellent. The “studio-quality three-mic array” is genuinely superb, and noise-canceling is good enough that when I was on a video call using the MacBook’s speakers and mic, my coworker thought I was wearing headphones. That does not happen on my M1 Air. [Image: Our review unit is silver, which is the only way to tell it apart from the space black models we tested in 2025 and 2024. It still comes in silver and space black. It still has three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, a 3.5mm headphone jack, an SD card slot, and the MagSafe charging port. Again, coming from an Air, that’s just nice. I love not having to find a card reader to import photos. I love having ports on the right side of the laptop. And I’ll never be mad at a headphone jack. The webcam is the 12MP Center Stage one Apple’s been using for the past few years, and it’s good enough. If I move around too much during a call, it can take a minute to recenter, but the resolution is good. It’s a huge step up from the one in my M1 MacBook Air. Battery life is still exceptional. The first day I had the MacBook Pro, I kept it plugged in because I was setting it up and running benchmarks. The second day, I unplugged it at 9:30AM and didn’t plug it back in until noon the next day. That’s over 12 hours of screen-on use, including about three hours of video calls and the usual multitasking. Hard to complain about that! [Image: [Image: The M6 chip found in the MacBook Pro is the same 12-core chip in the M6 Mac Mini and iMac, with two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores. It’s more than enough power for regular use, up to and including photo editing, the occasional video editing, and light gaming. All three M6 machines had very similar performance in nearly all our benchmarks. The exceptions were Premiere Pro, Photoshop, and DaVinci Resolve benchmarks, where the 24GB of memory in our Mini review unit gave it a 5 to 10 percent edge over the iMac and this MacBook Pro, both of which have 16GB of memory. Apple Silicon remains capable as hell. The MacBook Pro handled everything I threw at it, and I rarely heard the fan except during video-rendering benchmarks and while playing Cyberpunk 2077. Even then, it’s a faint white noise-y whoosh rather than the irritating whine of many laptop fans. Cyberpunk has recently been updated for Mac, with better MetalFX support and frame interpolation. Gaming on a MacBook keyboard is not really my idea of a good time, but I’ve played a lot of Cyberpunk on my desktop, so I’m familiar with the game. With upscaling and fake frames it’s tolerable on the MacBook in a pinch, but the game really wants more powerful hardware. I also ran into a few graphical glitches, including one that turned everyone’s skin bright green. That was fun. [Image: The silver color is a little more forgiving than black. Last year, we said the base M5 MacBook Pro, with 16GB memory and 512GB storage, was enough for most people. But that laptop cost $1,599 at the time; the M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 with 16GB of unified memory and 1TB of storage. I’m not going to complain too much about the price increase because it’s happening everywhere; that’s just the weather these days. Can’t do anything about it. It does put the base model MacBook Pro in a tight spot, however. MacBooks last a long time. Apple Silicon in particular holds up very well; every time we review a MacBook, we hear from people who are still perfectly happy with their M1 Pros or M1 MacBook Airs. My work machine is an M1 MacBook Air with 16GB of RAM. It’s getting a little long in the tooth — especially compared with the M6 I’m typing this on — but it’s hanging in there. Apple Silicon ages so gracefully that if you’re considering this particular MacBook Pro, you’re probably either coming from a very old Intel MacBook, or you’ve outgrown an older Air and you want more ports, a bigger screen, and better everything (or you’re switching over from Windows). If you’re considering spending upward of $2,000 on a new computer, you’re probably going to keep it for a while. And if that’s the case, you should get more than 16GB of memory. You’ll feel the lack of RAM before you feel the processor age. Now, if you’re running local AI models, doing high-res video encoding or 3D rendering, you should go straight for an M5 Pro or Max model with as much RAM as you can afford. You also don’t need me to tell you that. But if you’re considering the M6 MacBook Pro — this laptop — you should still get more RAM. Even if you don’t need it today, in five years you’ll wish you had it. But jumping from 16GB to 24GB of RAM without upgrading the storage or the screen puts you at $2,199; going to 36GB costs $2,399. And here’s where you hit the upsell. That’s only $100 less than the M5 Pro model with 24GB of RAM and a more powerful CPU and GPU. And at that point, you’re only $400 away from the one with the OLED. [Image: Is this the last we’ll see of the mirror logo? The best time to plant a tree is 20 years ago, but the best time to buy a laptop is next year. The M6 MacBook Pro is a fantastic laptop at a good price — RAM and storage shortage taken into account. But it’s also likely the last of its kind, and if you’re considering buying one but it’s not an emergency, you might be exactly the person who should wait for next year. Mark Gurman reports that next year’s entry M7 MacBook Pro will use the redesigned hardware of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. That chassis is a little bit thinner but nearly half a pound lighter, which makes a difference when you’re carrying around all the time. As my colleague David Pierce points out, the touchscreen part is whatever, but the OLED screen really is good. If you’re considering the M5 Pro or Max model, it’s worth spending extra for the redesigned model. If you buy the M6 MacBook Pro today, you’re still getting a great all-rounder laptop that’ll last you the better part of a decade. Everything about it is good to great. You can’t go wrong. But if your current laptop still works and you think you’ll want the thinner, lighter OLED model, you might consider holding out just a little longer. Apple has shown us it can make an even better MacBook Pro; I can’t wait to see what next year’s looks like. Photography by Nathan Edwards / The Verge --- Apple MacBook Pro 14 M6 specs (as reviewed) * Display: 14.2-inch (3024 x 1964) 120Hz Mini-LED * Processor: Apple M6 (12 CPU cores, 12 GPU cores) * Memory: 16GB unified memory * Storage: 1TB SSD * Webcam: 12-megapixel Center Stage camera with Desk View * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 * Ports: 3x USB-C / Thunderbolt 4, SDXC card slot, HDMI 2.1, headphone / mic combo * Weight: 3.4 pounds * Dimensions: 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61 inches * Battery: 72.4Wh * Price: $1,999

articles.title: The touchscreen MacBook Pro is a winner
articles.summary: Apple’s latest high-end MacBook Pro has an OLED display, a lighter and thinner body, and plenty of performance. The touchscreen works well, but you won’t use it much.
articles.body: I keep forgetting the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display has a touchscreen. I’ve been testing this new laptop, one of the most impressive Apple has ever created, for the better part of a week. I can’t stop noticing some of its other features: the slimmer design, the improved display, the Dynamic Island that somehow catches my eye more than the notch ever did. But I keep forgetting that as I go about my day, I can now reach out and poke the screen. Come to think of it, that might be exactly what Apple intended. Steve Jobs said touch laptops were a bad idea; some subset of users demanded one anyway. Now the MacBook Pro has one. But not in a way that meaningfully changes the laptop experience. There have been a few times I have found the touchscreen genuinely useful, better or more intuitive than anything I could do with a trackpad or a mouse. But to call this “the touchscreen MacBook Pro” just doesn’t feel right. It’s the latest evolution of Apple’s most powerful laptop — and oh, it happens to have a touchscreen. Very little about this laptop, or my experience with it, will come as a surprise. That’s a good thing; the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display (which I will just be calling the PROLED Pro from now on, because ugh, the name) comes with a bunch of new upgrades but no new problems, and performs as well as you’d expect from a laptop this expensive. Combine the screen, the body, and the touch, and you have something like a new generation of MacBook Pro. It’s going to be a good one. [Product: Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display | The 14-inch PROLED Pro starts at $2,899, and the 16-inch at $3,399. Both come with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip, each with two configurations to choose from, plus a bunch of RAM and storage options. It’s a lot of options! (My review unit is a 14-inch model with an M5 Pro chip that has 18 CPU cores and 20 GPU cores, plus 48GB of RAM and 1TB of storage. Total cost: $3,699.) In general, this device runs about a $400 premium over the standard, similarly specced Pro, but spoiler alert: I think it’s worth it, touchscreen or no touchscreen. If you buy the fully loaded PROLED Pro with the beefiest M5 Max chip, nano-texture glass, 128GB of RAM, and 16TB of storage — at a whopping $14,549 — you are my hero. And I have some questions. My middle-of-the-road PROLED configuration benchmarks almost exactly in line with other devices running an M5 Pro, such as the most recent Mac Mini. One simple way to think about Apple’s M-series chips is that the cores get faster with every generation, and you get a bunch of additional cores (and faster memory) with the Pro and Max chips. So on a single-core, one-task benchmark, the M5 Pro comes in slightly behind most M6 devices, even much cheaper ones. But as you get to more complex computing tasks, particularly anything involving the GPU, the M5 Pro and Max brute-force their way to better performance. That means the M5 Pro and Max suit anyone doing heavily graphical work or local AI development. The tests prove these laptops are very fast, which we already knew. They also prove they’re just as fast despite being inside a machine that’s smaller and thinner, which is not always a given. Apple says it redesigned the thermals inside the laptop both to accommodate the new design and to direct heat away from the OLED display, which can degrade or even fail if it gets too hot for too long. The Pro’s fans always seem to turn on before the laptop even gets a little hot — that’s clearly deliberate on Apple’s part. [Image: The smaller bezels and Dynamic Island make the screen look even more impressive. As for the OLED itself, it’s gorgeous. The slimmer bezels and smaller cutout make it loom even larger and more central in the laptop; it has almost that iPad-like, “magic pane of glass” feel. It’s sharp and contrast-y, gets both very bright (though it only hits peak brightness under very specific conditions) and very dim, and is better even than the very good screens on Apple’s other laptops. Visual professionals will need, and appreciate, the fidelity to P3 and Adobe’s RGB color spaces; the rest of us will probably most notice just how much more dramatic the blacks look as we play games or watch movies. I generally live in dark mode, and it looks even better on this machine. One theme of Apple’s recent product launches has been how much thinner an OLED display is than an LCD, and what that means for the product as a whole. What it means, mostly, is that the Apple logo can glow again. But also, just as OLED made it possible for the iPad Mini to shrink even more, the PROLED Pro is smaller than its predecessors by an impressive margin. My 14-inch model is a fraction of an inch smaller in every dimension than the standard MacBook Pro, which is always a good thing, but the half-pound weight decrease (more than two-thirds of a pound on the 16-inch model!) is what really impresses me. At 3 pounds on the dot, the 14-inch PROLED Pro is closer in weight to the 15-inch MacBook Air than the 14-inch MacBook Pro. It still feels solid and dense, but I appreciate the slimmer build every time I pick it up or toss it in my backpack. The only small downside of this new design, at least to my ears, is the speakers. The Pro’s built-in speakers have always been impressive, but I find the new model a bit bass-heavy and roomy. Everything sounds like it’s playing in a large, empty warehouse. Still, these are better speakers than you’ll find in almost any other laptop. Most of the rest of the hardware hasn’t changed. Same three Thunderbolt 5 ports, same HDMI and SD card access, same headphone jack, same keyboard, same trackpad. Even the battery life seems about the same: I get through a pretty heavy workday with a third or more of the battery left. I would always like more ports, especially on a device with this much raw multitasking power, but this appears to be the selection Apple is going with. Give it a year or two, and I suspect every model in the MacBook Pro lineup will look like this. The OLED display, and the smaller and lighter laptop it enables, are such obvious upgrades that Apple would be silly not to bring them to other devices. Do you need to pay the $400 premium just to get them right now? Probably not. But next time you’re in the market for a MacBook, get one with the new screen and the new look. [Image: Oooh, glowing. So far, we’ve talked about a bunch of things that add up to a better MacBook Pro. If there’s a big new idea about computing in here, it’s the PROLED Pro’s touch support. For the first time ever, the Mac has a touchscreen. The mental model for that touchscreen is very simple: It’s a mouse emulator. When you tap on the screen, the Pro registers it like you’ve clicked the mouse or trackpad. In theory, this should work everywhere; in practice, it works almost everywhere. In a few instances, in particular while playing games, I’ve encountered a button that simply would not respond to touch. And since there’s no touch equivalent to hovering your cursor over a notification or icon, there are a few things you just can’t do with a tap. I can swipe away a notification with a tap, but I can’t make the X appear in the corner to quickly dismiss it. Apple made a couple of tiny changes to macOS to accommodate touch, like the automatically expanding traffic lights for managing windows, but that’s about it. If developers choose, they can add all sorts of other touch controls to their apps, allowing you to use multiple fingers at a time or do complicated movements you never could on a touchpad. There’s very little of that now, of course, and I wouldn’t expect it anytime soon. Given that only this one top-of-the-line model supports touch, only the pro-est of pro apps are likely to find it worthwhile to support this Pro. For as long as we’ve been talking about touch Macs, the obvious problem has always been that macOS is not suited to touch. All the buttons are small! I might tap the wrong things! I am here to tell you that all those worries are both entirely correct and largely irrelevant. It makes no sense to use touch as a primary navigational tool on the Mac, to constantly move your hands back and forth between screen and palmrest. And so you won’t. You won’t tap between Excel cells, either, or start dramatically swiping through your email. Even if you love the touchscreen, you’ll use it a lot for a day or so and go back to using your laptop almost exactly the way you did before. [Image: The touchscreen is a mouse emulator and nothing more. The Dynamic Island is a good example. I like having both the Dynamic Island and Live Activities on the Mac — it’s easier to control music from there than to find my open Spotify tab, and I like seeing sports scores while I’m working. But I never tap the thing. Technically, you can get to Siri by swiping down from the Dynamic Island (though dragging with the trackpad doesn’t work for some reason), but I never do that. It’s so much more work, and half the time I end up accidentally moving an app window instead. Even a feature borrowed from a touch device works better with a mouse on this device. That’s not to say the touchscreen doesn’t come in handy, though. It does more often than I expected. When I’m editing photos, reaching out and spreading my fingers to zoom in on the section I want to see is vastly easier than clicking and dragging with the trackpad. When I’m watching a movie, I can just tap the video rather than wiggling the mouse to find the cursor. My favorite touch use so far has been when I’m showing somebody something on my computer — now we can both swipe between options or tap to make an edit rather than having to crowd around the trackpad. That all adds up to maybe a half-dozen taps on the touchscreen a day. Which I think is plenty. I tried, very briefly, to use the PROLED Pro like a touch-first device, and found it essentially impossible. There’s no onscreen keyboard that appears when you tap a text box; you don’t get the copy / paste / select all pop-up when you tap on words. No radius of tools appears when you tap the Apple Pencil on the screen in Procreate, because, oh wait, the Apple Pencil doesn’t work at all. You can tap on the Dynamic Island to control the currently playing music, or swipe from the edge to see your notifications and widgets, but those are the most touchscreen-native things about this computer. [Image: The traffic lights are one of the only touch-friendly parts of macOS. You can see where this all might go if Apple decides to make touch a truly core part of the MacBook. You’d want a laptop with a more flexible hinge so you can flip the device around into more touch-friendly positions. You’d want all the Mac’s system interfaces to be a little bigger and easier to tap. You’d want apps to be very Mac-ish and very iPad-ish all at the same time. You’d spend the rest of your life wiping fingerprints off the screen. Frankly, I don’t think I want any of those things. I don’t think Apple wants them either. Ultimately, the PROLED MacBook is just not a touchscreen laptop. It’s a laptop that happens to have a touchscreen. Since Apple first announced the PROLED Pro, I’ve heard from and read about a lot of people who have been waiting for this upgrade. If you bought a MacBook Pro in the last couple of years, I don’t think you need to throw your computer in the trash and buy this one instead. (Though I’ve heard Apple is offering pretty hefty trade-ins right now…) If you bought, say, a model from the M1 generation, I’d bet that laptop is holding up just fine but maybe beginning to show its age. If that’s you, and you want a new computer that’s going to last you just as long as the last one did, the PROLED Pro is the one to get. If this is really what the future of MacBook looks like, we’re in for a generation of fabulous laptops — whether you want to touch the screen or not.

articles.title: Aina's smart ring has a screen, a joystick and a mic so you can talk to AI agents | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Aina's ring can also take calls and help you dictate notes on your Mac.
articles.body:
Hardware startup Aina released a smart ring today that features a screen, a joystick, and a mic so that you can talk to your agents and take notes. The $399 ring has a speaker so you can take calls using it as well.

The startup, which raised $5.5 million in July , is positioning the ring as a controller of sorts for both AI and non-AI apps.

The company previously made Mirage, a three-key controller that let you invoke buttons based on the app on your Mac’s screen. For instance, if you were on a Google Meet call, you could map keys to camera on/off, mic mute/unmute, or to leave the meeting.

Aina has baked in lessons from that device to create the new ring, which it’s simply calling “AI ring.” Using its mic, you can take notes, send a prompt to agents, set reminders, and dictate notes on your Mac using Wispr Flow or the startup’s own dictation engine.

Now, there are already smart rings in the market that do similar things, like the Pebble Index 01 , Sandbar Stream , Oasis , and Natura , which is probably why Aina has added more controls and functionality to stand out. Its ring comes with a speaker so that you can take calls, and there is a screen, which lets you see notifications from your phone or which apps you are controlling.

For navigation, there is a joystick, and it also supports gestures, so that it can trigger different actions based on what’s on your Mac or phone’s screen. The ring also lets you control music or even smart home devices like Apple TV.

I have used the ring for a few days, and it feels like a smartwatch in a ring format with more controls. I can get notifications and reply to them. It surfaces my meetings; I can call Uber if I want to get a ride home.

It’s easier to use Apple TV’s remote itself, but the Aina ring proved useful the couple times I couldn’t find the remote. Granted, a lot of the software and features are still being fleshed out, so it’s hard to figure out where such a device ring might sit in my daily usage, but it is squarely aimed at folks who are surrounded by digital devices and AI applications.

“Phones and laptop screens were designed for an age of browsing where you think about opening apps. For interacting with proactive agents, we need a better interface, and that is what we had in mind while designing Aina,” Apoorv Shankar, Aina’s founder, told TechCrunch over a call.

Companies are trying to cater to programmers and AI enthusiasts with specialized hardware that could help them harness different agents. This includes OpenAI’s experimental keyboard and Rabbit trying to position itself as a controller . The hope with such hardware is that enough people will have multiple agents running to invest in specific gadgets to keep tabs on them.

Aina’s ring goes on pre-order starting Thursday at early-bird pricing of $399, and the company plans to start shipping the device in January 2027. Once the early-bird period ends, the ring will cost $499.

articles.title: Camp Snap made a smaller kid-friendly version of its retro digital camcorder
articles.summary: Camp Snap miniaturized its CS-8 retro digital camcorder so it’s lighter and easier for kids to use.
articles.body: After introducing new color options for its screen-free CS-8 video camera last month, Camp Snap announced a miniature version today that’s less than half the size of the original. The new CS-8 Mini carries forward the retro design of the larger version that was inspired by Canon and Kodak Super 8mm film cameras from decades ago, but features a smaller grip that’s easier for smaller hands to hold, and a step down in resolution. While the original can capture 4K videos, the Mini’s 1/2.7-inch sensor is limited to 2.7K. [Image: The CS-8 Mini is launching in blue, green, pink, and orange color options. The CS-8 Mini is available now through Camp Snap’s online store and Target for $149.99 in bright blue, orange, pink, and green color options. There’s still no screen, no Wi-Fi 0r Bluetooth connectivity, and no app to download. The Mini captures video to an included 4GB microSD card using a trigger-style recording button that creates a new clip every time it’s pressed. Videos are downloaded to other devices either using a card reader or a direct connection with a USB-C cable. [Image: Camp Snap redesigned the CS-8 Mini’s battery and storage meters to use LEDs. The Mini is designed to be easy and accessible for kids, but still includes a decent number of recording options borrowed from the larger version. There are four aspect ratios to choose from including 16:9 widescreen, 9:16 vertical, 1:1 square for easier sharing on social media, and 4:3 emulating a retro home movie aesthetic. There’s also up to 8x digital zoom available plus five film-style filters. In addition to a standard mode there’s two vintage looks, an analog option that goes heavy on film grain and flickering, and black and white.
